description: Team FireLens is tackling the Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots challenge. We’re building a web app that merges NASA FIRMS fire records into one consistent burning-activity calendar for any area on Earth, and flags satellite outages so missing data isn’t mistaken for no fire. Our skills: Python, Streamlit, geospatial data and machine learning.
summary:
A sudden fire broke out near my home in La Habra recently, and it made me want to understand wildfires. But when I looked at NASA's satellite fire records, I found a problem: in 2027, NASA's MODIS satellites, the yardstick for 25 years of fire history, stop collecting data. Their replacement, VIIRS, records about 4.5 times more fire hotspots, so old and new records can't be compared directly, and questions like "is this fire season worse than normal?" become hard to answer.

MODVIIR is a web app that harmonizes the two. Built on more than 267 million NASA FIRMS hotspot records from 238 countries and territories, it calibrates MODIS onto the VIIRS scale, country by country and month by month, and tests itself on years it never saw: median error fell from 81% uncalibrated to 20%, beating a single global conversion factor (33%). Users get a burning-activity calendar from 2000 to 2025, can compare any month with its historical median, and can download the data.

MODVIIR also knows when a satellite goes dark: during California's 2024 Park Fire, it marks VIIRS outage days "not observed," not "no fire." An experimental AI model also forecasts next-day hotspots in California.
details:
WHY I BUILT THIS

A sudden fire broke out near my home in La Habra recently, and it made me want to understand wildfires. When I started analyzing NASA's satellite fire records, I found that the record is about to split in two.

THE PROBLEM

For 25 years, fire managers and national monitoring programs have answered "is this season worse than normal?" by comparing against NASA's MODIS fire record. NASA plans to end Terra MODIS data collection in January 2027 and Aqua MODIS around September 2027. The successor, VIIRS, sees smaller fires at finer resolution and records about 4.5x more hotspots worldwide (2019–2025), so mixing the two records without calibration creates false trends.

WHAT I BUILT

1. Harmonized burning-activity calendar: for any of 238 countries and territories, a year-by-month calendar from 2000 to 2025 on a single VIIRS NOAA-20 scale: observed values from April 2018 onward, MODIS-based modeled values before that, each with an 80% uncertainty band.

2. "Worse than normal?" panel: compares any month with its historical median and ranks it among all years, with a small-count guard so tiny countries don't show misleading percentages.

3. Continuity check: a chart showing the MODIS-based estimate tracks what VIIRS actually recorded in the overlap years.

4. Gap-aware evidence (2024 Park Fire): a record-level inspector showing 208 of 316 Park Fire evidence groups were MODIS-only during a documented VIIRS S-NPP data interruption (July 24–28). MODVIIR treats those days as "not observed," not "no fire."

5. AI next-day hotspot forecast (California): a ConvLSTM neural network learns from 7 days of satellite hotspot maps to predict where hotspots will be recorded tomorrow on a 10 km grid. Compared with assuming "tomorrow = today," it caught more hotspot cells with 22% fewer false alarms. Against the strongest simple rule ("active on at least 3 of the last 7 days"), it caught 17% more hotspot cells at nearly the same precision (F1 +0.030, 95% block-bootstrap CI +0.022 to +0.038, 285 days in 2025). It was trained on MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP, the very sensors now retiring, which is why AI models also need harmonized records. This is retrospective research on a previously inspected test period, not an operational warning system.

6. CSV downloads of calendars, validation tables and evidence records.

HOW I VALIDATED IT

I calibrated MODIS against VIIRS NOAA-20 using country-month records from complete overlap years (2019–2025), then used leave-one-year-out testing: each year was predicted by a model trained only on the other years. Across 13,225 held-out country-months, median error fell from 80.7% (uncalibrated) to 20.4% (monthly country ratio), beating a single global ratio (33.0%) and a region-shrunk regression (21.5%). A placebo test on 150 Amazon days showed a MODIS-based daily estimate would carry about 32% median error, so I chose not to "fill in" outage days. 47 automated tests check the pipeline.

HONEST LIMITS

Values are satellite hotspot records, not fire counts or burned area. 2000–2002 modeled values are likely low (Terra-only MODIS). The global calendar works at country level; arbitrary areas need daily global archives. Data runs through 2025.

WHAT I WANT TO DO NEXT

Daily global calibration for any user-drawn area (like my own neighborhood), near-real-time FIRMS updates, and automatic outage detection.

TOOLS

Python, Streamlit, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly, pyproj (EPSG:6933 equal-area grids), Shapely, PyTorch (ConvLSTM training), GitHub Actions for automated tests. I used AI assistants for coding and writing (see Use of AI).

NASA DATA I USED

I used NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) active-fire archives: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Terra/Aqua, 2000–2025) and VIIRS 375 m NOAA-20 (2018–2025) yearly country archives (34 files, 267,356,689 records, 238 countries and territories), plus MODIS and VIIRS S-NPP regional archives for the Amazon (2022–2025), California (2022–2025) and the July 2024 Park Fire. I kept only FIRMS type-0 (presumed vegetation fire) detections. NASA's documented VIIRS S-NPP data-interruption notice and the FIRMS missing-data dates identified the July 24–28, 2024 outage.

MY RESEARCH JOURNEY AND THANKS TO NASA

Before this hackathon, I was already researching wildfire detection on my own. In September and October 2026, I sent 30 initial emails asking about satellite observations, thermal imagery, drone technology and useful datasets: 12 to university professors and researchers (including at Caltech, UC Berkeley, UCLA, UC San Diego and UPenn), 17 to fire department contacts, and 1 to a NASA researcher, plus 2 follow-ups. Through that search, I kept looking for one thing: a long-term, consistent record of where and when fires burn. NASA FIRMS turned out to be exactly the data I had been looking for. Its openly available MODIS and VIIRS archives let me work with more than 267 million satellite-detected vegetation-fire hotspots, something no student could collect alone. Working with this data was a truly valuable experience, and I am grateful to NASA for making it free and open to everyone.
